content: Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is indicated for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in patients aged 12 years and older with compensated liver disease. The recommended dosage is 25 mg orally once daily with food. Prior to initiating therapy, patients should be tested for HIV-1 infection, as tenofovir should not be used as monotherapy in patients co-infected with HIV. Baseline and periodic monitoring of serum creatinine, phosphorus, estimated creatinine clearance (CrCl), urine glucose, and urine protein levels are recommended throughout treatment. For pediatric patients aged 6 years and older weighing at least 25 kg with compensated liver disease, the same dosage of 25 mg orally once daily with food is recommended. Safety and efficacy in children under 6 years of age have not been established. Drug Interactions with Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF): 1. Enasidenib: Enasidenib increases the levels or effects of TAF by inhibiting transport proteins such as OATP1B1, OATP1B3, and BCRP. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the dosage of the affected substrate according to its prescribing information. 2. Lenolisib: Lenolisib, a BCRP inhibitor, increases systemic exposure to TAF. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 3. Letermovir: TAF decreases the levels or effects of letermovir via P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. Co-administration with P-gp inducers is not recommended. 4. Sotorasib: Sotorasib decreases the levels or effects of TAF via P-gp efflux transporter. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. If unavoidable, adjust the dosage of the P-gp substrate as per its prescribing information. 5. Tepotinib: Tepotinib increases the levels or effects of TAF via P-gp efflux transporter. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. If unavoidable, reduce the dosage of the P-gp substrate as recommended in its product labeling. 6. Acalabrutinib: Acalabrutinib increases TAF levels by inhibiting intestinal BCRP. Use caution and monitor closely for adverse effects. Dosage adjustments of BCRP substrates may be necessary. 7. Apalutamide: Apalutamide decreases TAF levels by increasing its elimination. It weakly induces BCRP and may reduce systemic exposure to BCRP substrates. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Berotralstat: Berotralstat increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Monitor or titrate the P-gp substrate dose if co-administered. 9. Cabozantinib: TAF increases cabozantinib levels, potentially leading to toxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. MRP2 inhibitors may exacerbate cabozantinib toxicity. 10. Danicopan: Danicopan increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. It also increases plasma concentrations of P-gp substrates. Consider dose reduction of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious adverse reactions. 11. Darolutamide: Darolutamide, a BCRP inhibitor, increases TAF levels. Avoid co-administration with BCRP inhibitors. If unavoidable, monitor closely for adverse reactions and consider dose reduction of BCRP substrate drugs. 12. Duvelisib: TAF decreases duvelisib levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Elagolix: Elagolix increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Encorafenib: Encorafenib, a BCRP inhibitor, increases TAF levels and toxicity. Monitor closely for signs of increased exposure and adjust the dose of BCRP substrates as needed. 15. Fostamatinib: Fostamatinib increases TAF levels by decreasing its metabolism. Monitor for toxicities of BCRP substrate drugs and adjust dosages as necessary. 16. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir: This combination increases TAF levels by decreasing its metabolism. Monitor plasma concentrations of BCRP substrates and adjust dosages as needed. 17. Ifosfamide: Co-administration with TAF increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Monitor electrolytes and renal function closely. 18. Istradefylline: Istradefylline increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Consider dose reduction of sensitive P-gp substrates. 19. Lonafarnib: Lonafarnib, a weak P-gp inhibitor, increases TAF levels. Monitor for adverse reactions and reduce the P-gp substrate dose if needed. 20. Mavorixafor: Mavorixafor increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Use caution when co-administered with sensitive P-gp substrates. 21. Momelotinib: Momelotinib, a BCRP inhibitor, increases TAF toxicity by competing for plasma protein binding. Monitor closely and adjust the dose of BCRP substrates as necessary. 22. Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir: This combination increases TAF levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely for increased systemic exposures. 23. Orlistat: Orlistat decreases TAF levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Monitor HIV RNA levels frequently in HIV-infected patients, as virological control may be lost. 24. Otesaconazole: Otesaconazole, a BCRP inhibitor, increases TAF levels and toxicity. Use the lowest starting dose of BCRP substrates or consider dose reduction. 25. Regorafenib: Regorafenib likely inhibits BCRP transport, increasing TAF levels and toxicity. Monitor closely for systemic exposure and related toxicities. 26. Safinamide: Safinamide and its metabolite inhibit intestinal BCRP, increasing TAF levels. Monitor for increased pharmacologic or adverse effects of BCRP substrates. 27. Sarecycline: Sarecycline increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Monitor for toxicities of P-gp substrates and adjust dosages as needed. 28. Stiripentol: Stiripentol, a BCRP transport inhibitor, increases TAF levels. Consider dosage reduction for BCRP substrates if adverse effects occur. 29. Tafamidis/Tafamidis Meglumine: These drugs inhibit BCRP and increase TAF levels. Dosage adjustments of BCRP substrates may be necessary. 30. Tucatinib: Tucatinib increases TAF levels via P-gp efflux transporter. Consider reducing the dosage of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities. 31. Vadadustat: Vadadustat increases TAF levels by increasing BCRP substrate exposure. Monitor for adverse effects and reduce substrate doses as needed. 32. Voclosporin: Co-administration with TAF increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Monitor renal function and electrolytes closely.
